We have now done that this morning and the statement was available to the Defence on the general EDS, and I think just to make the point that we disclosed without checking the EDS because our understanding is that under 68(ii) with respect to -- to giving a collection a searchable format, if we come across something that we have actual knowledge of should be disclosed, despite whatever is on the EDS, we would go ahead and disclose it, and that's why we took that step yesterday. So this may change Mr. Stojanovic's position with respect to any future application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think his concerns went beyond what was said --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one second. We printed EDS system, searching for this document, and it wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now perhaps that was exactly what I suggested, that you would, during the break, meet and see to what extent your information is -- is affirmed. Perhaps you have used different search term or whatever. But I still encourage you, before making any written submissions, to exchange whatever information there is. We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, before the witness is in, because we don't need him for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were discussing about Dusko Tadic's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And -- 1D273. We have it as 1D273 in the system, if we can see it on the screen. And we can see the date and the page and line numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if you think, I can quote it to the witness if you think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we need to have it in evidence if you can -- if you limit yourself to quote. Although, with the last portion I would have an observation there, but I'd rather not do it in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll continue, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We left off with a document - please bear with me for a moment. We were talking about whether there was artillery or not. And then on the second page --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the document is not in e-court. Its 65 ter number is 18348. In the English version, it's the last paragraph on the second page. In B/C/S, also the last long paragraph at the bottom of the page, where it says: "The rump BH Presidency held a meeting on the 9th of April 1992 and placed all armed elements, excludeing the JNA and the MUP, under a single command."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know today, or did you know at the time, what were the armed elements that the rump Presidency placed under its command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were Territorial Defence units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. All the volunteer units were incorporated into the TO Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am excluding the territory of the Banja Luka Corps and the north-east Bosnia in the direction of Brcko. In the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Territorial Defence was set up and those units were incorporated into it. They purchased weapons from JNA members, amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the document accurate where it says that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina invites officers and civilians to leave the army and join their ranks. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the person who drafted this document was Colonel Mesud Hasotic. I never wanted to socialise with him because he was an extremist. I even didn't want to read his documents, including this one, because I did not agree with his opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we have mentioned Hasotic's name, he is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he hails from Sandzak, and until the very end of the war he stayed with the Banja Luka Corps because his son lived in Novi Pazar, so he feared for his life. And I understand fully why he acted in this way. He was fearful for his son's life.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was going on in Novi Pazar to make him so fearful for the life of his son?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over there, the police of the Republic of Serbia, there was an operation and everybody knows what they were capable of. If Hasotic did not behave adequately in the Banja Luka Corps, there would have been consequences. A lot of bad things happened. People were beaten up and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you never read his reports. Did you socialise with Colonel Hasotic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. He came into my office once or maybe twice throughout that whole time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- can I stop you there. We started with a question about the content of the document. We're now dealing with the socialising and whether his son was living where and why he was afraid. But I would like to have an answer to the question. The question was: Whether, to your knowledge, the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina invited officers and civilians to leave the army and to join their ranks. That was the question. If you know, tell us; if you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I know that's true. There was requests for the officers and civilians to leave the JNA and to join the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now that was the question, Mr. Selak. You started telling us that you didn't want to socialise with the author of the document. Why not just answer the question? Apparently a simple yes would have done. And, Mr. Lukic, if the witness does not answer the question, try to take him back and do not follow him in straying away from what you apparently wanted to elicit from him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll just have to -- still to follow what he said, because he said this is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said it was -- he now says it was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. Yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. At the time he didn't say it's not true. He said I didn't read it is because I didn't like him, et cetera, et cetera. He didn't say a word about the quote you gave. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me finish with just one more question. Did Colonel Hasotic tell you personally that he was afraid for his son's life, which is why he drafted the documents in the way he did?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember where that information came from. However, my other colleagues had an adequate opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer is, no, he didn't tell you personally; isn't it? Because that was the question, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember whether he was the one who told me that or not. I can't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about your son? Was he a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My older son was a doctor and he was mobilised into the medical corps of the Banja Luka Corps in 1992. And, yes, he was a member. Until the moment he went to Belgrade and then onwards to Germany where he still resides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up -- or, rather, before that, I would like to tender this document into evidence. Its number is 18348. We had a rather lengthy discussion about the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 18348 shall be assigned Exhibit D52. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D52 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to call up 1D281 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a transcript page from the Brdjanin trial dated 20 January 2003, and the page number is 13202. On line 11 --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in English, what I have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is just for the Judges. I'm going to read that for you? The question is this. I'm going read to read that for you. The question is this -- I'm going to read in English and the interpreters will interpret it for you. [In English] "It's correct, isn't it, that prior to 1991, according to your estimate, about 90 per cent of the officers in the JNA were Serb? Immediately prior to 1991." [Interpretation] Your answer was: [In English] "No. I think that 90 per cent were of the Serb and Montenegrin ethnicity, and there is also official information to that effect." According to you, were 90 per cent of the members, as you stated at that time, would you say the same thing today?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I made a mistake. It was about 70 per cent. I had incorrect information. In my satchel, Your Honours, I have a census from 1981 and from 1991, and we're talking about 70 per cent of Serbs and Montenegrins. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Further on, on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D282, which is also a page from the Brdjanin case transcript, and the page number is 13203, 20 January 2003, in lines 5 through 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman asked you: [In English] "By the end of 1991, that percentage had increased to 99 per cent Serbs; [interpretation] is this correct?" And you say: "Yes, yes." Would you say the same, that by the end of 1999 there were 99 per cent of Serbs in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In July, 1991, there was a mobilisation for the JNA and only the Serbs responded. The Croats and the Bosniaks did not, those who resided in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that had an enormous impact on the ethnic composition of the JNA. People who had failed to respond to the call-up, both Muslims and Croats, were brought in by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, if you say 99 per cent, is this a precise calculation or is it just a general impression that almost all of them were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an estimate. I'm talking about the Banja Luka Corps and the logistics base. And that was the kind of composition we had. It -- it was a -- an estimate. There are very few Croats and Muslims among the officer cadre, but no soldiers at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, I asked this question to the witness because often he expresses himself, as far as numbers are concerned, in a way which is -- well, not -- I would say is not the accurate number but is more of an impression. For example, if he says that Sanski Most is closer to the border than Banja Luka, looking at the map might learn you -- might teach you otherwise. And whether it's 25 or 30 kilometres, or perhaps 50, that's -- so the Chamber will understand these matters unless you clarify it as rough estimates expressing more a general view than precise numbers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The growth in percentage, as you stated it yourself, the growth in the participation of Serbs in JNA units in the territory of the corps that you belonged in was a consequence of the war in Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that that had an impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you say that people were brought in, Muslims and Croats were brought in by the police for not responding.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I issued wanted notes against some of them. That was in July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So they were called by the army, but they turned the call down?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because they did not consider JNA their own army as a result of the politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter number 2838.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document was issued during the war, on the 1st of June, 1992. Page 2 in this document, which is 1 in English, towards the very end of the page, refers to the heaviest fighting which took place in the area of Hambarine, Prijedor, and Kozarac. We are coming back to Prijedor, although it is already the month of June. It says here, on line 7, which is the following page in English, on the top of page 2, it says: "Among those who were arrested, there is a number of officers and organisers of paramilitary formations." Did you know then, or do you perhaps know today, which officers are referred to in here? Were there any members of the JNA among them or were those some other officers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this involves Zarko Tole, Colonel Zarko Tole, a Croat, and Stanic, Anto, a Croat also. They were former members of the JNA who had joined the HVO at that time, in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time did you know anything about infiltrated groups in the territory that was covered by your corps? At that point in time, it was already the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, at a meeting at the corps command -- or, rather, at all meetings of the corps command, regular information was provided to officers about that. I attended these meetings, and that's why I received this information. So, yes, I was kept abreast of all of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bear with me, Your Honours. I'm trying to go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Yugoslav People's Army left Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 18th of May you requested retirement. From that moment, you became a member of the Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, later on the Army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because all units of the JNA were renamed into the Army of Republika Srpska, including my logistics base. The one that I commanded. But I immediately submitted a request for retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I now please have in e-court 1D278.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the Brdjanin trial, the 20th of January, 2003, and transcript page 13181. We need lines 8 through 12. Again, I'm going to read this out in English so that you would receive a correct interpretation. [In English] "And in that connection, being a Serb army, it would not be unusual or improper or out of line for there to be a legitimate concern about the loyalty of non-Serb officers, would it?" And your answer, in line 12, was: "I agree?"

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question or?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, not yet. Now, line 16. And when you say is this a question, I can ask you, actually, whether you'd said this today as well. And this would be normal procedure for an army to ask for its members to be loyal?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every army on the face of the earth asks for loyalty from its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, if they're not loyal, is it surprising or strange that they don't want to have them in their ranks any longer?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are other measures too. Disciplinary measures. And also re-training, re-education.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, on this same page, can we look at pages 16 through 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were appointed as the liaison officer with UNPROFOR before you asked for retirement; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in March 1992. But I had been dismissed because I lacked political eligibility or, rather, ethnic eligibility. There's a document here, Your Honours, where the corps command states that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this hostile corps command, what position did they assign to you after you had been dismissed, as you said? Which position did you go to then?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to the position that I had left before taking up this post, so that's commander of the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see. So was this some kind of punishment? What was your understanding of that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lack of confidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And they returned you to be commander yet again?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't pension me off. It was only logical for them to return me to the post I'd held.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You yourself said that other measures could have been taken. They could have also taken your rank from you. They could have demoted you. They didn't do any such thing; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they could have liquidated me too, but there was no reason for that. I behaved fairly, honestly, and in a proper, professional manner as commander of the logistics base. So there's no reason for disciplinary measures. But it was a question of political eligibility, not professional, and that is what this document says. That was signed by General Talic. Because of that kind of lack of eligibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they demote you? Did they strip your rank?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing. They returned me to my post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a moment, please. My colleague, Mr. Ackerman, also ask you whether you had any problems while you served in the Army Republika Srpska as a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I personally did not have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please take a look at 1D279. It's also from the Brdjanin trial. 13183 is the page reference. The date of trial is the 20th of January, 2003. There's a reference to General Uzelac. And it says that he was always in this group of leaders of the SDS, that they had dinners and other parties. And my colleague, Mr. Ackerman, asked you, from page -- or, rather, line 17 onwards: [In English] "And this group that was out at dinner parties almost every night where all the decisions were made actually wanted you to join them, didn't they, to become part of that group?" And your answer, at line 21, was: "That is my understanding, yes."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that this lack of confidence that was expressed to you, or was it you who expressed a lack of confidence in the group that asked you to join them?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Crisis Staff of Banja Luka involved Serbs only who held high positions in the Bosnian Krajina. They lived in Banja Luka at the time, and, indeed, they did meet several times in a restaurant. Once I was present as well. General Uzelac invited me. When I what it was that was discussed, I decided I no longer wished to attend so that I would not be seen communicating with such persons. Because I did not agree with that policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is: Is it correct that they trusted you and that they wanted to have you with them?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not trust them and that you did not want them with you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I didn't trust them. I didn't agree with the topics that were being discussed and the drinking that took place, these large amounts of alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you tell us, Witness, what the subjects of discussion were, so that we better understand your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these were political topics about the breakup of Yugoslavia, that certain political parties and groups wished to break up Yugoslavia. That is what was discussed, as well as national policy. Especially what was going on in the Bosnian Krajina, because the Crisis Staff covered all of the Bosnian Krajina, and it was the highest organ of government at that point in time in the Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it -- national policy, could you explain what you meant by that? What was the gist of the national policy they discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at those meetings, I never saw a single Croat. I was the only Bosniak there. This seemed symptomatic to me. Because there were others who held higher positions than I did in government and in other organs of authority, and I wondered why they were not invited to these gatherings. This carousing, if I can call it that. That would be an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if I understand you well, then your answer is you felt uncomfortable in company where there were only Serbs and where other Croats and Muslims were apparently not welcome. Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Now I would kindly ask that 65 ter 18349 be called up in e-court, please. I have to ask the Prosecutor for clarification. This was not supposed to be under seal, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe so. But in an exercise of caution, could we have the witness look at it because it relates to him personally and perhaps he can tell us whether there's any problem with it being shown publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So not to be broadcasted at this moment until the witness has said anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you go to a private session first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, you know best what you wrote and why you wrote what you did in this document, but I'm not going to ask you to explain to us. This introduction, for instance, where it says the information from the period 1991 through 1995 is from the region of Banja Luka. Is that the period you covered in this letter?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 you say, I'm providing a list of information, in bullet points. "In mid-May 1991, the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was armed and equipped as resistance to the order of General Uzelac for arming the Serbian population in the municipalities of the Banja Luka region. This is why I asked General Jovanovic, assistant commander for logistics, to remove me from the post of commander for logistics. I did not issue any weapons, but that caused me personal problems later on ..." What kind of problems did you have, Colonel, because you did not obey the order of your superior?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Uzelac was not my superior. I was subordinated directly to the 1st Military District in Belgrade and General Jovanovic was in Belgrade. The units that required weapons -- in fact, the units for which they required weapons, were not linked to the entire force. Only the Serbian force. That's the information I had. And Uzelac was not able to give me orders to supply weapons because he was not my superior. And that later caused problems between me and General Uzelac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of problems; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because these units were --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I only want to know what kind of personal problems you had.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just for example, General Uzelac invited me the regular briefings before at the time when they began; whereas, after that, he invited me for one hour after the beginning. So obviously they wanted to discuss certain things without me and they avoided contact with me in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to clarify this now, although we've already discussed it, but you are making me revisit the subject. And you say again that Uzelac was not your superior?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were not on his staff or his command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your presence was not obligatory?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was normal for you to come when he invites you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the understanding was that I should attend their meetings to hear about the problems related to logistics so that I could tell my organs to speed up their work to address those problems, not to go through administration and correspondence because that is much slower. That's why they invited me to these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you don't attend when you're not invited; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, from that time on I was still invited but with a delay?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that the same Uzelac who invited you to dinner parties, the one you are now having problems with?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had invited me before. After this point, he never invited me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So after May 1991, he never invited you again?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that I ever attended one of their parties again. The priority parties certainly not. Some of the official meetings, yes. But he liked alcohol. Everybody who knew him knew that, and his entire company liked to drink. I simply didn't belong in that company, and I'm happy about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman discussed with you the time when there was the Army of Republika Srpska already in existence, and I also understood when examining you today that you were talking about the same period, that they were inviting you to those dinner parties after 18 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 18th of May? You say that I stated that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it follows from the questions and answers. Because you talk about the Crisis Staff and other --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never attended sessions of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the group of people, including members of the Crisis Staff and General Uzelac. That group extended invitations to you. You were testifying in Brdjanin about that period. Are you talking about the same period today when the Army of Republika Srpska already existed in the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th December 1991, General Uzelac left Banja Luka. He got a transfer. When the Army of Republika Srpska was established on 18 May 1992, I had quite normal official and private contacts with my colleagues from the corps of the same rank, same level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber considers that it is sufficiently informed about this matter at this moment. So would you please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I plan to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next you say, under para 2, fifth bullet point. It's still page 2 in B/C/S. That's page 2 in English. You say: "The transport of artillery ammunition from Donji Vakuf to the Ustikolina depot, a barricade of the HDZ in Vitez. That the ammunition had arrived from Slovenia and Croatia. On that occasion General Uzelac passed on the order that vehicles had to go through, otherwise there would be air-raids. At the office of the PSO, chairman of the Municipal Assembly of Vitez, Ivica Santic, I received the same order on the phone from a colonel, head of the technical service of the 1st Military District, Ivo Pantelic." Tell us, what is this PSO Santic, Vitez?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: President of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "I phoned the PSO of Vitez, Ivica Santic," does it mean the same thing?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does "gen" mean?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just give me the context, I'll tell you. Maybe it means "general," maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now? "The transport of artillery ammunition ..." You can't see this part of the page where it's deleted. Now you can see it. The word here was "gen," and then it's stricken through and PSO.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had made a mistake. First of all, I said general, but Santic was, in fact, the president of the municipal assembly in Vitez. That was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You go on to say: "Along with this, at one point when we were alone, I shared with him some information. After that, I spoke to him several times on the phone from Banja Luka, meaning with PSO Vitez, Ivica Santic, who thanked me and invited me to visit him." Did this Ivica Santic later receive a rank?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no clue, Your Honours, whether he got a rank. He was a civilian, president of the Municipal Assembly. Why would he need have a rank? I see no reason whatsoever. He thanked me because there could have been an explosion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Simple question, did he receive a rank later? I have no clue. That does for an answer. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that there was a general, Ivica Santic in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was a general, Ivica Santic in Bihac. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear of it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of information did you provide to Santic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that because the ammunition, live ammunition and air bombs and mines and explosives were transported from Croatia to my ammunition depot in Donji Vakuf, and we were keeping this dangerous material in open air. I informed the command in Belgrade about the problem and the danger it posed when such things are kept in open air, and I asked that my ammunition be moved to Ustikolina near Foca, which is Eastern Bosnia, the border with Serbia where there was a large ammunition depot. One member of the HVO, Dario Kordic, who is now serving his sentence, organised the blockade, a roadblock in Karnik [phoen] to stop this column from passing. The general told me to go there urgently and solve the problem. And I told Santic, if there's an explosion it will kill many people because these are explosives we are dealing with. That's what the conversation was about, and I was there when he realised that, and then I got orders from Belgrade to tell Santic if they don't let the column through, the air force would bomb Vitez municipality. That was the issue. And the column passed through. The Minister of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Avdo Hebib, came to help in the negotiations, and the column was escorted to Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next bullet point begins with the words: "In September ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, it's on page 2. The third bullet point from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, all of the Judges are lost as far as the relevance of all this. We see that it's apparently a letter with information passed to the son of the witness and then to be available to others. But what this has -- what the relevance is for the charges in the indictment is totally unclear to us at this moment. So if you put questions, try to do it in such a way that had the Chamber does understand the relevance of those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'll try to ask a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know what you wrote here, that you had ordered a simulated explosion in the depot contrary to Uzelac's orders, that you chose a man of confidence, a captain, and ordered him to simulate an explosion in the depot, and there are more examples of the same kind. So I'm asking you, is it true that more than once you acted against the interests and the orders of the then-Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am proud of this. Because the Banja Luka Corps, or, rather, the leadership of the Yugoslav People's Army ordered the commander of the 5th Military District -- in fact, when he withdrew to Banja Luka he ordered me, following orders from Uzelac, to get all the fuel out and ammunition from Karlovac and to set mines to the installation, to the depot. I went there with a team of experts, and I didn't agree with it. But I saw that tank trucks from Serbia transporting fuel, and I stopped that attempt to explode, to blow up the depot. Somebody from -- from -- from the top came to inspect. I told them that I made preparations to blow the place up, but I was -- I was lying. I hadn't done that. In the same way, I stopped the blowing up of the -- of the hospital because they wanted to do that only because the units of the JNA were leaving. The hospital in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to speak a little more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Selak. Mr. Lukic, if you would ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Lukic, your last question was a bit confusing because it was a composite question. You asked whether it was true whether he acted against the interests and the orders of the then Yugoslav Army. You can act in favour of the interests and against orders, you can act in favour of the interests and following orders. That -- it's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well I'm not -- I think from the answer of the witness I understood, but please correct me when I'm wrong, Mr. Selak. I did understand your answer to be that to the extent you may not have always followed orders, it was in order to avoid dangerous situations. Is that short -- a short summary of your answer? Would that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And the damage to the economy of Yugoslav in the area of Croatia, because that was a crime. It would be a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you again say to Mr. Mladic he should not speak at a volume which is heard by others in this courtroom. I hear it through my earphones. He should stop doing that. Because we [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what he says and earlier today the witness complained about it. So it's really the last warning in this respect. At the same time, I'm looking at the clock. It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- time for a break. Then whatever is there to be discussed can be discussed during the break. And if after the break you want to further deal with the matter, then you are, of course, free to do so. But otherwise please move on. And could I ask you whether - already inviting the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom, a break, Mr. Selak - Mr. Lukic, are you on track as far as your cross-examination is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I should finish by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And try to focus on the most relevant matters. We take a break and resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Selak, we'll still dealing with that letter of yours. And the first paragraph on the second page of the B/C/S version, so we need page 2 in B/C/S. In the English version, it's page 2, the fourth bullet point from the top. Let me not read all of it now. You say that what had been ordered was to deal with a factory in Hrvatska Dubica, to quickly dismantle it you sent an expert team with a captain, a mechanical engineer, a trustworthy man of yours who stated in his report that the factory was fully intact and fully operation. You say I did not allow the machines to be dismantled and because of that the command of the 5th Corps and the political leaders of the SDS caused me a lot of problems, threatened me, and so on. This factory, why was it important? Why was it important to dismantle it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was in Croatia and they wanted it to be dismantled and sent to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It wasn't of a military nature.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was purely civilian materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were other occasions where you disobeyed orders?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not obey the order to blow up the military hospital in Zagreb and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How come? Are you a mining expert? Are you an engineer? How would you get this kind of order to blow up a factory in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, yes, I had specialists for ammunition who worked for me, who were under my command, and they were the ones who dealt with this anywhere at any time. De-mining, I mean, explosive materials and so on. So it's only the base that had that, the corps did not have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we are not talking about de-mining here. We are talking about mining.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could your people also blow things up, or were they experts for de-mining?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they are experts for de-mining, then of course they can do the opposite as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who are these people that you entrusted with this task of de-mining?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the hospital, Your Honours, I would kindly ask you -- I mean, for the military hospital in Zagreb, I would kindly ask you to provide information that's a bit more extensive. The chief of security of the military hospital in Zagreb, Captain Jovanovic - I don't who gave him my telephone number at the office - he called me and asked me comrade, Colonel, Colonel Nikic is in the military hospital, that's the director of the military hospital. The Croatian forces have surrounded the military hospital and I have carried out preparations to have the military hospital mined. If I am attacked do allow me to blow it up, the military hospital. Your Honours, according to the Law on the JNA, an officer, if he cannot reach his superior officer, then the next person up the line of seniority takes over all responsibility. He was a captain. Somebody gave him my telephone, said I was a Colonel. He asked me that. I thought this was a provocation, and I said I will not allow you to blow up the military hospital. I reported that to the General Staff in Belgrade, and they gave orders to General Raseta in Croatia in Zagreb, and he was the one who was negotiating with the Croatians, and that is how things turned out with the hospital. That's what I had to say about the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I leave it in your hands. I mean, you raised the issue. You asked questions about it. Again, what we are supposed to do with all of three's details and whether -- how far away it is away from what is charged in the indictment. I leave it to you, but ... As we always said before, we closely will monitor the way in which cross-examination is conducted. We'll continue to do that when granting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a fact that this witness mentioned the military hospital in Zagreb without any questions being put op our part, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you should stop him, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you something in relation to this hospital in Zagreb. We have to round this off. How come somebody called you from Zagreb in relation to the mining of the hospital? I don't understand that at all. Why is it that they called you? What do you have to do with that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I give a precise answer to this question. And that is as follows. I was president of the automobile association in Banja Luka and there were races, automobile races. The Yugoslav championship. One of the participants from Croatia took part in the military hospital -- took part in the championship and worked as a driver in the military hospital in Zagreb. He had my telephone number, and then Captain Jovanovic got my telephone number from him and phoned, because the law says if you cannot reach your immediate superior, if you can reach any officer who outranks you then that person takes over responsibility. So I took over responsibility and I did as I reported to you a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is speaking at a rate that is too fast for interpretation and court reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I already tried to slow the witness down. You really should slow down, Mr. Selak. Otherwise your testimony will be lost, and that's not what you want, is it? Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this letter, you refer to a person called Karabasic as a particularly negative person in addition to General Talic. That's what you say in this letter. Who is this Karabasic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is Captain Kasabasic. Yes. How do I put this? What was negative was that he liked to have a drink too many, liked to stay away from work, and politically he also knew how to be negative. If I can put it that way. And that's not only what I though to Nikola Kasabasic but other colleagues thought that too. I think it's Nikola Kasabasic. I'm not sure. I've forgotten. But I think it's Nikola Kasabasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then we get to this part where you say -- or, rather, we've already discussed this. I'm not going to ask you for the names of these persons. The court has already ruled on this. You say that a command was formed for opposing the Serb army in the region of Banja Luka and I was commander of that. I don't want to name any names, but could you tell me whether in this organisation there were any former officers of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not correct. Armed resistance, no. No armed resistance was planned because the Banja Luka Corps had over 100.000 men. The SDS had blown up the mosque 15 or 20 days earlier on in order to provoke the Muslims into reacting. We concluded in this resistance staff that we would not do anything in a military way but that we would advise people to flee and join the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so there was no armed resistance. It's only that we tried to save people. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just read this out from your own letter, and it says armed resistance here in your letter.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I made a mistake. There was no armed resistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- again, Mr. Mladic, if you want to consult, low voice, low volume, nothing else. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you whether there were any officers of the JNA, former officers of the JNA with you in that group.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how many members did this group have?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you suggested to people to leave Banja Luka and to join the TO BiH, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you communicate? How did you send these messages of yours to the population, to people?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I lived in Banja Luka, and these colleagues of mine lived in Banja Luka. These were personal contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Personal contacts.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time did you report to the other side about movements of units? Were you involved in intelligence work for the other side?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reported about what was happening and about the crimes that were being committed in Banja Luka. Your Honours, during the course of the war in the town of Banja Luka itself, over 300 persons were killed and thrown into the Vrbas river. In addition to that, Muslims and Croats were ordered to leave Banja Luka and to sign over their apartments, saying that they would not ask for their immovable property to be returned to them. Your Honours, I have a document to that effect here with me as well. This document in which they would sign over their property and say that they would never ask to have it returned to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, at the time did you report to the other side, what did you consider at the time? After the witness had retired or when he was still in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify with the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I understand that it was after. After his retirement. But maybe I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, my question is what did you mean by "at the time." You meant after he had --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which then -- when you said about reporting, about people were killed, et cetera, that was after you had left the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. From the 15th of July, 1992, Your Honour. That's when we established this resistance movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And by "the other side," you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Either Croatian army or Army of B and H.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Other to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Other than the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I ... Please, put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd briefly like to go back in time because I'm dealing with all the things that are still pending so we will try to conclude all of this. We talked about the referendum on independence. Could we please have in e-court 1D274. This is the trial of Dusko Tadic. The 5th of June, 1996, is the date. This is what I'm interested in. From the beginning of the page, you mention that Colonel Cendic, Radislav, suggested two units, men and soldiers, I believe, how they should vote. And then the lawyer asked you: "How did he tell them to vote? And your answer was: "To vote against the referendum, against the independence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Was that the official position of the JNA at the time, to vote against the independence of any republic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Cendic was precisely in favour of that, voting against the referendum. Rather, against the cessation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was his position and that what is he carried out with his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the question was whether he expressed the formal position of the JNA? Was that the official position of the JNA he expressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. To stay in Yugoslavia, yes, with a view to staying in Yugoslavia. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have now answered the question. Please, Mr. Lukic, the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you vote, Colonel Selak?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my very own private affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D275. Could we have that briefly in e-court, please. This is also the trial of Dusko Tadic. 1247 is the page reference. I would be interested in lines 32 and 33. And one more line on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out. This is what is written here. The question is -- the question of the lawyer was: [In English] "To your knowledge, in the spring of 1992, did the paramilitary units in the Banja Luka area come under the command of the military?" [Interpretation] Next page now. Your answer was: "No." Would you say that to this day, that paramilitary units were not under the control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not, Your Honours, under the control of the JNA, but JNA units armed them and allowed them to train in the training grounds at Manjaca near Banja Luka. The Red Berets and other units. Their command was at the Bosna Hotel in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that you've brought this up, can you tell us who it was that made up this command; do you know?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have established, and you told us, that you did not supply Keraterm with food or anything else. Is it also correct that you did not supply Omarska either? Either with food or anything else.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need to wrap up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just give me half a minute to consult, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, just one more question: Could you explain whose orders did you obey?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1991, 1992. Beginning with September 1991 until you were retired on 7 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders from the command of the 1st Military District in Belgrade and in Sarajevo, because they took turns. They took turns. The headquarters were -- was first in the 1st Military District, then in the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo. So I obeyed the orders of the assistant commander for logistics of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of these persons in the 1st and 2nd Military Districts?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. People changed. There was several colonels from Croatia who came and then they were killed, unfortunately. Then they were replaced. I can't remember. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crncevic was in Belgrade but I don't know who was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Jerko Crncevic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Crncevic was in Belgrade. He is in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking, Mr. Mladic. Now this is really the last warning. And it's of no use to make gestures that you apologise. You should refrain from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Jerko Crncevic was a Croat by ethnicity, this man who worked in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose, judging by his name. But I don't know really because I did not communicate much with him, talked to him a couple of times on the phone and I wasn't interested in his ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Groome, is there any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how much time would you approximately use?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think I might be able to finish today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, over the course of the last three days you've been asked about many, many different topics. I want to explore just one topic with you that was raised by Mr. Lukic on Tuesday. It raised at transcript page 3030. It has to do with the illness of your wife. And first let me remind you of your answer in response to a question posed by Mr. Lukic. "Q. Did you leave Banja Luka in spite of this? "A. Yes. In 1995, when my wife fell ill, I asked General Mladic to allow me to leave and to go to Belgrade to the Military Medical Academy in an ambulance. "Q. Was this made possible for you? "A. I phoned General Djukic. He put me through to General Mladic, and he said that he ordered Colonel Marjanovic to take me to Belgrade." Do you recall those questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I apologise for asking you to return what is undoubtedly a difficult and sad memory, but I do want to ensure that the record correctly records your evidence on this event. And I would like to do this by asking you a few very specific questions, each requiring a short answer. First, can you please tell us, if you know, what was the position of General Djukic at that point in time when you made the request?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djukic said he could not issue any orders himself without General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me just -- if I could direct you to the very specific question I'm asking you: What was his title or what was his position, if you know, at the time that you made the request?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was assistant chief of the Main Staff for logistics in the VRS. He was my direct superior in the Army of Republika Srpska. My colleague from the academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've just said General Djukic said he could not issue any orders himself without General Mladic. When did he say that to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment when I called him up. I can't remember the date now. It was in the month of May, I think, 1992. Because my wife was ill at the time, I was upset ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, on Tuesday, the record recorded you as saying your wife fell ill in 1995, and now I see you've been recorded as saying 1992. Which year did your wife become ill and did you make this request?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, then it must be a mistake. My wife fell ill in May 1994. She had a surgery in Banja Luka, a tumour was found on the colon, and she was taking cytostatics and she was sent in 1995 to the military medical academy because the doctors were unable to give any guarantees in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at the time that you made this request to General Djukic, do you know where he was physically located. Where was his office?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Djukic was at the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, at Pale, near Sarajevo, and his telephone number had the city code 011, which is the code for Belgrade, and he had that phone in -- in Pale. That's the number I used to call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You testified that Djukic put you through to Mladic. Do you know where General Mladic was physically located at the time that you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Pale, in the same office. That's where they met. He just passed on the receiver.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us the command structure between General Mladic and General Djukic at that time? In other words, was Djukic a direct subordinate of Mladic, or were there other levels of command between them?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was directly subordinated to General Mladic because General Mladic was commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, whereas Djukic was assistant commander for logistics in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us precisely what it was you were asking? Were you asking for permission to transit areas under the control of the VRS, were you asking for ground or air transport to Belgrade, or were you asking for something else? What specifically were you requesting?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I specifically requested that he order Colonel Marjanovic, chief of the medical service of the Banja Luka Corps, to take an ambulance that was constantly shuttling to and fro from Belgrade to take my wife to Belgrade. He probably wasn't able to do that without the orders of General Mladic, and he asked me to get orders from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you described this act of General Mladic as an order. You said: "He ordered Colonel Marjanovic to take me to Belgrade." My question to you is the following: When you used the word "order," did you intend it to mean order in the sense of a military order of a superior to a subordinate?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean military order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Selak, I want to be careful how I phrase my next question, and I want to be sure that you didn't misperceive it to the difficult time that you were facing, both you and your wife. What I want to ask you is the following. When you called Djukic to ask for assistance in getting your wife to Belgrade, did you expect that the decision to assist you would require an order from the commander of the Main Staff himself?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was sure because it was all about me not leaving Banja Luka because of my wife, and General Mladic had to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Any further questions? I think Mr. Mladic would like to consult with you for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would you allow me just a few minutes to explain something during this consultation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. First of all, during the consultation, we should not proceed. That's one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, your mike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could ... I -- I -- Mr. Mladic, I see you're trying to do your best to lower the volume of your voice, but you should not only try but even succeed in avoiding that someone else hears it. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Colonel, at that time there was an embargo against Republika Srpska from the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was talk about an embargo, but there was communication between subordinates and superiors. The VRS could only exist with the help of the Republic of Serbia and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said Republika Srpska, not the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want the transcript to be true. Were you aware of the procedure for any transport or the wounded or patients to move to Belgrade? Whose permission was required?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wounded and patients who could not be properly treated in Banja Luka were sent in ambulances for treatment to Belgrade and that worked on a regular basis. And Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- even told me plaintively that did he not have enough room for my wife because there was so many wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of that colonel you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Marjanovic. I can't recall his first name. A doctor of medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you if you were familiar with the procedure which papers needed to be submitted so that these wounded and ill people could be transported to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All medical care for members of the army took place through the medical corps in Banja Luka, if we're talking about members of the army. If they could not get treatment in Banja Luka, they were sent to Belgrade, to the Military Medical Academy, or to some other hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your wife was not a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But she was my wife. She was a family member. She was entitled to treatment at the Military Medical Academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And she was, indeed, sent there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Marjanovic did write the papers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you should abide by the instructions as well. Apart from how important this matter is, or whether it's marginal, before we start asking about at what speed exactly the ambulance drove to Belgrade, please try to focus on important matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm finishing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you knew that Mladic had to be -- had to decide. But you're not calling Mladic. You're calling another person. Why do you call another person if it's up to Mladic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djukic, as assistant commander for logistics, was superior to Colonel Marjanovic? I called up General Djukic, and he, then, connected me with Mladic. I don't know what passed between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And General Mladic allowed it.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said, I'll give orders to Colonel Marjanovic. I called him two days running. The first -- once and then two days later, and still the order was not obeyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well, that, finally, after one phone call or after two phone calls, that Mr. Mladic agreed that your wife could be transported to Belgrade and gave the relevant orders for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what General Mladic told me. Because I spoke to him directly. Whether he had, indeed, given orders or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did Marjanovic tell you? What did Marjanovic tell you? Did he get a call from the general? Did the general give his permission? Did you discuss it with him?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went with him to the infirmary, and he told me then, There's no room in the transport because there are too many wounded. And, in the end, I had to pay 2800 Deutschemark from my own pocket so that my wife could be transported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was your last question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I didn't say that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Selak, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, and I wish you -- not only for coming but also for answering the questions that were put to you, and I wish you a safe return home again and good health.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I had only asked you for a minute or two. Your Honours, in 2002 this APB was published in Republika Srpska. I'm wanted as a war criminal for testifying in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, you were examined here as a witness. That means that questions were put to you. You've answered those questions, and even sometimes went beyond what you were asked. If there's anything important and relevant which you consider should be known to this Court, then I invite you to bring that to the attention of the Office of the Prosecution so that they can further look into the matter, consider the relevance of it, and try to find ways to bring it before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you can bring it to the attention of Mr. Groome. Again, I wish you a safe and healthy return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. No comment, Mr. Mladic. And we do not start counting tomorrow at one. We start at five or six, where we are now, as far as consequences are concerned. For tomorrow, the next witness is available and doesn't require any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is Mr. Crncalo which is scheduled for 30 minutes from what I understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that we will be able to conclude the testimony of the next witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. My colleague Ivetic will do -- cross-examine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just in terms of scheduling, I would like to update the Chamber on the 92 bis as soon as possible because I will be asking for some further guidance so that we can keep our work progressing, so could I ask, if possible, if we needed stay an extra five or ten minutes to do that. My submission I'm pretty sure can be done in less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we can do it at some point tomorrow, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, to the extent possible, would you try to finish tomorrow half an hour before the end of the session. And I see Mr. Ivetic is pretty confident that he will be able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If he says so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He nods even so. Mr. Groome, that would meet your --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. And then thank you for my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, Friday, the 28th of September, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of September, 2012, at 9.30 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.18 p.m.,
